exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect malignant otitis externa rather than simple otitis externa? — Severe otalgia, otorrhea with granulation tissue, diabetic background, possible cranial nerve deficits.
Which imaging modality best assesses skull‑base involvement and why? — MRI with gadolinium; it visualises soft‑tissue spread and nerve involvement better than CT.
How does uncontrolled diabetes affect the pathogenesis of MOE? — Impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis, promotes Pseudomonas growth, and delays healing.

If culture results are unavailable, what empiric antibiotic regimen should you start and why? — An anti‑pseudomonal IV agent (e.g., ciprofloxacin or ceftazidime) because Pseudomonas is the predominant pathogen.
What cranial nerves are most commonly affected and what clinical signs would you look for? — VII (facial weakness), IX/X (dysphagia, loss of taste), XI (shoulder droop), XII (tongue deviation).
When is surgical debridement indicated in MOE? — When there is persistent necrotic tissue or abscess despite adequate antimicrobial therapy.

How would you monitor treatment response in a resource‑limited setting? — Serial ESR/CRP trends, repeat otoscopic exam for granulation regression, and bedside assessment of pain and cranial nerve function.

Why is it important to differentiate MOE from chronic suppurative otitis media? — Management differs: MOE needs systemic anti‑pseudomonal therapy and possible skull‑base imaging, whereas CSOM is usually treated with topical antibiotics.
ai.title: Malignant Otitis Externa
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Chronic infection of the external auditory canal that spreads to skull base, seen in diabetics and immunocompromised patients. Early recognition, targeted antibiotics and monitoring prevent serious complications.

b: Not a true cancer; ‘malignant’ refers to aggressive behaviour.
Typical organism: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
sections.p: Malignant otitis externa is a necrotizing infection of the external auditory canal that can extend to the temporal bone and skull base. It occurs mainly in elderly diabetics or patients with impaired immunity.

b: Risk factors: uncontrolled diabetes, chronic renal failure, HIV, long‑term steroids.
Typical presentation: severe otalgia, otorrhea, granulation tissue in canal, cranial nerve palsies if advanced.
sections.p: Diagnosis rests on a combination of clinical suspicion, imaging and microbiology. The disease is staged by extent of bone involvement (temporal bone only vs skull‑base spread).

b: Mortality rises to 30 % with skull‑base involvement.
Cranial nerves VII, IX, X, XI, XII may become palsied.
sections.p: If untreated, the infection can cause skull‑base osteomyelitis, cranial nerve deficits, meningitis and death. Prompt antimicrobial therapy and surgical debridement when needed are lifesaving.

t.b: Identifies causative organism; guides antibiotic choice. If unavailable, start empiric anti‑pseudomonal therapy.
